title: Hymns inside the letters
hookLine: Philippians 2, Colossians 1, 1 Timothy 3:16: early Christian songs embedded in letters
tomorrow: wives, children, slaves: the hardest lines in the letters. now what?

lines: A TOAST TURNS INTO A CHORUS.
cards: A wedding toast is going fine: thank-yous, a story about the groom, a joke about the dog. Then the speaker stops talking and starts the chorus of the couple's song, and the whole room says it with her.
First Timothy does something like that.

In the middle of instructions about church leaders, the prose changes step: "God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory."
Short lines. A beat you could clap to. Why would a letter suddenly sound like a song?

teach.b: The letters never stop to say here's a hymn. Readers hear it in the shape: lines that balance, fall, and rise. Philippians two is one place people point to.
Christ "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant." He goes down, all the way to "the death of the cross."
Then the line turns and climbs: "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him," "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow."
Down, then up, like a melody. Did these churches sing? The letters say so.
Colossians tells them to teach one another "in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs." And Acts puts Paul and Silas in a jail cell: "at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God."
So here's the solution some readers offer.
When a letter breaks into rhythm, Paul may be quoting what the church already sang, the way a speaker drops in a line the whole room knows by heart.
The letters don't say that outright; it's a reading of their shape. But if it's right, the singing came first, and the letters caught some of it on the page.

how: Churches sing and read passages like Philippians 2:6–11 in worship, and some hymns and worship songs set its words of going down and being lifted up to music.

games.q: a friend in your Bible study says hymns are just decoration, and the real teaching is in the letters' plain sentences. what might Philippians 2 suggest?
o: she's right; songs and teaching never mix in scripture.
some of the letters' teaching may itself be a song.
hymns only came into worship long after the letters.
games.why: some readers hear Philippians 2:6–11 as a hymn the church already sang, quoted because everyone knew it. if so, the teaching and the song are the same lines.

practice: Find Philippians two, verses six to eleven, and read it aloud, slowly. Let your voice drop as the lines go down to the cross, and lift where they turn: wherefore God also hath highly exalted him.
Then sit with the echo for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Hymns inside the letters. Passages with the balance and beat of a song, which some readers think the churches sang before the letters quoted them.

orig.note: Greek: a hymn, a song of praise. It appears in Colossians 3:16, "psalms and hymns."

carryVoice: Your line: they sang before they wrote. Some of what the letters teach may have had a tune first. See you tomorrow.
